text:
The history of Nike and the real Nike story: how a college runner selling shoes out of the trunk of his car and his old track coach built the biggest sports brand on Earth, without owning a single factory. This Nike history documentary covers Phil Knight, Bill Bowerman, Blue Ribbon Sports, the waffle iron, the 35 dollar swoosh, Michael Jordan and Air Jordan, Just Do It, the sweatshop scandal, and Nike's comeback plan under Elliott Hill.

Nike brings in more than 46 billion dollars a year, about 127 million dollars every single day, yet it owns almost none of the factories that make its shoes. L.A. Gear went bankrupt, Converse went bankrupt and was bought by Nike, and Reebok has been sold twice, but Nike is still here.

This documentary follows the complete history of Nike: Bill Bowerman and the University of Oregon track team, Phil Knight's Stanford paper on Japanese running shoes, the 1962 trip to Onitsuka in Kobe, Blue Ribbon Sports, selling shoes from a car trunk, Jeff Johnson and the first store in Santa Monica, Bowerman's Jogging book, the waffle iron sole, the Cortez, the split with Onitsuka, Carolyn Davidson and the 35 dollar swoosh, Dimension Six and the name Nike, the swoosh ring and stock, the Moon Shoe and the 1972 Olympic trials, Nissho Iwai, Steve Prefontaine, the 25 million dollar customs bill, Frank Rudy and Nike Air, the 1980 IPO, Tinker Hatfield and the Air Max, the Beaverton campus, Nike's asset light business model, Vietnam manufacturing, Reebok and aerobics, Sonny Vaccaro, Michael Jordan and Deloris Jordan, the Air Jordan "banned" myth, Jordan Brand, Just Do It and Wieden and Kennedy, Bo Jackson, the 1990s sweatshop scandal, Tiger Woods, Converse, LeBron James, Flyknit, Shoe Dog, Vaporfly, Colin Kaepernick, Eliud Kipchoge, John Donahoe's direct to consumer strategy, the Dunk, On and Hoka, Elliott Hill and the Sport Offense, fiscal 2026 results, the Pace restructuring, the 2026 World Cup, and ASICS.

Everyone says Netflix killed Blockbuster. That's not really what happened.

In 2000, Netflix offered to sell itself to Blockbuster for $50 million and got turned down. That part is true. But a few years later, Blockbuster had a hybrid DVD-by-mail and in-store service that genuinely had Netflix worried. text:
The Economics of Owning a Chicken Farm

Chicken is the most eaten meat on the planet — roughly nine billion birds a
year in the United States alone. And over the last seventy years, while almost
everything else in the grocery store got more expensive, chicken got
dramatically cheaper.

That kind of efficiency never comes from nowhere. Somebody paid for it.

Here's the part most people don't know: you can own a chicken farm, run it for
twenty years, and never own a single chicken. In the modern poultry industry,
the company owns the birds, the feed, the medicine, and the genetics. The
farmer owns the buildings, the debt, the fuel bill, and the manure.

In this video we break down the real economics of owning a chicken farm: the
tournament pay system that ranks farmers against their own neighbors, the
million-dollar buildings with exactly one possible use, the twenty-year loan
signed against a contract that can end after the next flock, and the reason
this arrangement became the template for how a lot of modern business now
works.

text:
The Economics of Owning a Data Center

On paper it's the perfect landlord business. Your tenants are Amazon,
Microsoft, Google and Meta. They sign leases measured in decades. They buy
their own equipment. And demand is so far ahead of supply that vacancy in the
world's largest market has been running under two percent.

So why are there finished data centers sitting completely dark right now —
steel up, cooling installed, racks bolted to the floor — earning nothing?

Not because of money. Not because of demand. Not even because of chips.

Because they can't get electricity.

In this video we break down the real economics of owning a data center: why
this industry measures in megawatts instead of square feet, the efficiency
number that quietly decides your entire profit margin, the years-long grid
queue that no amount of money can skip, and the highest-margin product in
infrastructure that almost nobody outside the industry has heard of.

Then we get into the part that reframes the whole AI race — because a data
center isn't really a technology business, and it isn't really a real estate
business either.

text:
In 1985, Ray was 35 and had a plan: a steady job at one company, a house with a yard, money in the bank earning interest, and a pension waiting at the end. It worked. So he passed the plan on to his son, Tom. Tom is 47 now, he followed most of that advice, and somehow the numbers don't add up the same way.

In this video we go through five pieces of money advice our parents swore by, and why they don't work the way they used to: keep your savings in the bank, stay loyal to one company, get any degree, buy a house as soon as you can, and the biggest one of all: the company will take care of you. Plus the updated version of each rule, and the one piece of advice that never changes.
